title: Moonlight Mile
full_review:
"Moonlight Mile" is a disjointed study of a New England family grieving the death of a murdered daughter. While writer/director Brad Silberling's follow-up to his 1998 supernatural romance, "City Of Angels," boasts a formidable cast, the film ultimately suffers from his inability to channel a profusion of subplots into an emotionally engaging story. The picture's overall lack of narrative focus does not, however, preclude genuine moments of poignancy, humor and synergy among cast members.

Set in the fictional town of Cape Anne, Mass., in 1973, the film revolves around Joe Nast (Jake Gyllenhaal) who has just lost his fiancee, Diana -- an innocent victim of a shooting at a local coffee shop. Joe finds himself living temporarily with the people who were to be his in-laws, Ben Floss (Dustin Hoffman), a real estate agent, repressing a tempest of anger and guilt over his daughter's death, and JoJo Floss (Susan Sarandon), a quirky writer whose muse was also counted among the casualties of the senseless crime.

Each embraces the bereavement process differently. Ben masks his grief with Yankee gusto, plunging into his work and cajoling Joe into partnering with him on a major deal that will make them players in the coming real estate boom of the late 1970s. JoJo retreats into sarcasm and dons an acerbic armor, repellent to any sentimental attempts at sympathy. Joe is adrift, unenthused about Ben's business proposal, but bound by an awkward sense of loyalty to him and JoJo. Haunted by dreams of Diana, Joe wanders aimlessly, his doe-eyed facade fractured by a dark secret weighing heavily on him.

When Ben sends Joe to the post office to retrieve the wedding invitations before they are sent off, he meets Bertie (Ellen Pompeo), a mail clerk whose pixie-like looks and firecracker charm inject the first signs of life into Gyllenhaal's otherwise flat-line performance. Bertie also bears the scar of a lost love: Cal, her boyfriend who has been MIA for five years in Vietnam. She keeps the flame of hope burning by moonlighting as a barmaid in a local watering hole owned by Cal before he shipped out, unraveling whenever the movie's title track by the Rolling Stones is selected on the jukebox. She, like the other characters, is tormented by an inability to face reality -- condemning herself (as do Joe, Ben and JoJo) to a prison of self-delusion.

Joe quickly falls for Bertie, and must weigh his deepening affections for her against his sense of duty to Ben and JoJo, who see him as their only tangible link to their lost daughter. Recognizing a soul mate, Joe confides to Bertie that he and Diana had secretly called off their marriage and had planned to tell her parents the day she was murdered. The situation is further complicated when Ben informs Joe that the big deal he is trying to close hinges on buying out Cal's bar, a move that would jeopardize Joe's already fragile relationship with Bertie. Wedged into this is Diana's murder trial, with Holly Hunter playing the Flosses' hard-nosed prosecuting attorney -- an uninspired performance that does little more than get another recognizable face on an already star-laden screen.

At the close of the court case, Joe delivers a protracted monologue which comes across as contrived and conveniently ties together all the narrative's loose ends. Ben finds inner reconciliation, JoJo resurrects her muse and Joe and Bertie drive off, literally, into the sunset.

Primarily a ghost tale -- the character of Diana (and, to a lesser extent, Cal) seems to cast a long shadow over the entire picture, yet little, if anything, about her is ever revealed. Toward the film's conclusion, Holly Hunter's character explains to Joe that the only way to secure a 'guilty' verdict is for his testimony to make Diana real to the jury -- Brad Silberling would have profited from the same advice.

While the film's overall conviction that facing the truth, however difficult, will set you free is morally sound, much of the message's effect is mired by competing story lines, which also undermine otherwise strong performances by Hoffman and Sarandon. Forgiveness of others, as well as oneself, is another positive theme explored.

Due to a shadowy, implied sexual encounter, sporadic profanity and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
